newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia chides NATO, adopts new security vision.
newsitem.headline: Russia chides NATO, adopts new security vision.

text.p: Russia, saying economic crisis and social upheaval at home pose a bigger threat than foreign aggression, adopted a new basic vision for national security on Wednesday to see the country into the 21st century.

President Boris Yeltsin, chairing the Security Council meeting that approved the document, said Moscow must at the same time tackle concerns raised by NATO's expansion into eastern Europe. But as the military prepared for May 9 Victory Day festivities, he also renewed vows to cut the vast armed forces.

The Kremlin urged the West to give ground in negotiations on a treaty to lay out a new relationship between NATO and Russia after senior officials failed to announce an accord after their latest talks and scheduled new talks in Moscow next week.

"The Concept of National Security was approved," the Kremlin press service said in a statement after a Security Council meeting including the prime minister, his first deputies and the defence, interior and justice ministers.

Kremlin spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky said the text, which Yeltsin described as a comprehensive political document laying down priorities for ensuring the welfare of ordinary Russians, covered "internal threats" and external aggression.

No details were published. Unnamed officials were quoted by Russian news agencies as saying the 30-page text stressed the need for economic recovery to head off social unrest and ensure public support for the new democratic, federal system.
"We want Russia truly to be a great power but at the same time a democratic power," Yeltsin told the Council.
Among internal threats to Russian security, the most bitter have been separatist forces among ethnic groups on its borders.
Yastrzhembsky said Yeltsin was ready to meet Chechen President Aslan Maskhadov after the long Victory Day weekend to seal a lasting peace after the 1994-96 war but set no date.
On external menaces, Interfax news agency quoted a Security Council official as saying the text noted certain states wanted "to weaken Russia politically, economically and militarily".
It did not name them, but Yeltsin singled out NATO's plan to offer membership this year to some former Soviet-bloc states in eastern Europe as a threat to Russia's security.

"We will do everything to minimise the consequences for Russia's security of a possible expansion of NATO," he told Krasnaya Zvezda, the Defence Ministry newspaper. The president said Moscow would strengthen ties with other former Soviet states such as Belarus, with China and with other neighbours.

Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov and NATO Secretary General Javier Solana said had they made some progress in treaty negotiations in Luxembourg but failed to announce an accord and agreed to meet again in Moscow next Tuesday.

With time running out for a deal by the target May 27 signing date, Yastrzhembsky said: "Much more effort is needed from NATO as a bloc and from its members to reach mutually acceptable formulae which would allow us to sign the document."
He added, however, that even if the May 27 deadline is missed, negotiations would not end.

Russia wants a say in decisions by the Cold War-era Western defence pact and a guarantee it will not advance troops into new members. Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic are expected to be offered membership at a summit in Madrid in July.

On the eve of celebrations of the 1945 victory, Yeltsin lavished praise on Russia's vast but impoverished armed forces, calling them the heirs not only of the Soviet troops who crushed Nazi Germany but of 13th century prince Alexander Nevsky.

But, the president, who will view a military parade on Red Square for the first time since the collapse of the Soviet Union, told Krasnaya Zvezda troop numbers must be cut and he would not print money to pay off backlogs in army wages.

Yastrzhembsky said Yeltsin would not interfere in government plans to cut the 1997 defence budget by a further 30 percent this week as part of an emergency economy package. The Defence Ministry has said the cuts threaten the forces' war readiness.
